titulo: Cenário 3 — Multi-Agent Research System (banco de treino)

questoes.pergunta: Eastbrook University Library runs a multi-agent research system built with the Claude Agent SDK: a coordinator delegates to web search, document analysis, synthesis, and report-generation subagents to produce comprehensive, cited reports for faculty. Every request runs the same pipeline: five web searches, analysis of the top ten documents, synthesis, then the report. Grant-compliance checks, which follow a fixed checklist, come out well. For open-ended questions such as "What is known about microplastics in Arctic food webs?", reports miss major threads: a 2022 dataset cited by most of the analyzed papers was never searched for or analyzed. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: The search subagent issues too few queries; raising the count from five to twenty per request would capture the threads that are now missing.
The document analysis subagent's relevance threshold discards papers that mention the dataset only in passing, so it never reaches synthesis.
Open-ended questions run through a pipeline fixed in advance, so threads found in intermediate results never become new subtasks.
The synthesis subagent has no instruction to detect gaps, so it never asks for the dataset that the analyzed papers kept citing.
questoes.explicacao: A fixed pipeline fits predictable work such as the compliance checklist, but open-ended investigation needs dynamic decomposition: subtasks generated from what each step discovers. Here the analyzed papers revealed a key dataset, yet no step could turn that discovery into a new search and analysis.
feedbacks: More queries planned upfront still cannot target a dataset nobody knew about until the documents were read.
The papers citing the dataset were analyzed and reached synthesis; the dataset itself was simply never searched for.
Correct. Prompt chaining suits predictable checks; open-ended questions need adaptive decomposition driven by intermediate findings.
Gap detection helps only if something acts on it; in a fixed pipeline no step turns a discovered thread into new work.

questoes.pergunta: Eastbrook University Library runs a multi-agent research system built with the Claude Agent SDK: a coordinator delegates to web search, document analysis, synthesis, and report-generation subagents to produce comprehensive, cited reports for faculty. For broad topics, the coordinator concatenates the outputs of about 14 document-analysis runs (roughly 90k tokens) in the order the runs finished and passes them to the synthesis subagent with the instruction "Write the synthesis." Reviewers notice that findings from the analyses in positions 5 to 10 are rarely cited, while the first and last few appear in every report. What is the flaw in this design?
opcoes: The synthesis subagent needs a model with a larger context window, so that 90k tokens sit far below its limit and each analysis gets equal attention.
The coordinator should first compress each analysis into a two-sentence summary, so the synthesis input is short enough to be read evenly.
The coordinator should pass only the key snippets each analysis flagged and drop the rest, so the synthesis subagent reads a far shorter input.
It is one undifferentiated block, with no key-findings summary up front and no section headers, so middle findings get less attention.
questoes.explicacao: Models reliably process the beginning and end of long inputs but may omit findings from the middle (lost in the middle). Placing a key-findings summary at the start and organizing the detailed analyses under explicit section headers mitigates the position effect without dropping coverage.
feedbacks: A larger window does not fix the position effect; the model already receives the whole input but attends unevenly to its middle.
Two-sentence summaries strip the numbers, methods, and attribution synthesis needs; the problem is how the input is organized, not its length.
Bare snippets lose the context (methods, dates, sources) that synthesis needs, and the shorter input is still an unstructured block.
Correct. A summary at the beginning plus explicit section headers counters the lost-in-the-middle effect.

questoes.pergunta: Eastbrook University Library runs a multi-agent research system built with the Claude Agent SDK: a coordinator delegates to web search, document analysis, synthesis, and report-generation subagents to produce comprehensive, cited reports for faculty. A librarian ran a named research session on teacher-retention studies that analyzed 40 PDFs from a shared folder. A week later, two of the PDFs were replaced with corrected versions after the authors published errata that changed a key table. The librarian resumed the session to finalize the report, and the report still cites the old table values. Which statement about this behavior is correct?
opcoes: Resumed sessions reread their source files automatically, so the old values must be coming from a cache inside the synthesis subagent.
The resumed session lacks context room for both versions; resuming it with a larger context window would let it reconcile them.
A resumed session can no longer be trusted after its sources change; the safe option is a new session that re-analyzes the 40 PDFs from scratch.
The resumed session still reasons from its earlier tool results; it must be told which two PDFs changed so it re-analyzes them.
questoes.explicacao: Resuming restores the earlier conversation, including tool results that are now stale; it does not reread the files. Informing the agent which documents changed allows targeted re-analysis of those two PDFs while the valid analysis of the other 38 is kept.
feedbacks: Resumption restores the earlier conversation and its tool results; it does not reread files, so no cache is needed to explain the old values.
Context size is not the issue: the session never loaded the corrected versions at all.
With 2 of 40 documents changed, most prior context is still valid; targeted re-analysis is cheaper than starting over.
Correct. After source changes, tell the resumed session what changed so it re-analyzes those files.

questoes.pergunta: Eastbrook University Library runs a multi-agent research system built with the Claude Agent SDK: a coordinator delegates to web search, document analysis, synthesis, and report-generation subagents to produce comprehensive, cited reports for faculty. To cut token use, an engineer proposes that the web search subagent's agentic loop send only the latest tool result in each request, dropping earlier search results and tool calls from the messages and adding a one-line note: "Earlier searches were completed." In a test, token use fell by about 60%. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Adopt it: the model only needs the newest result to choose its next query, and a 60% token reduction is a large saving per report.
Adopt it, as long as the system prompt lists the queries already run, which gives the model enough to avoid repeating searches.
Reject it, and instead send only the original task in each request, letting the model rerun any earlier searches it still needs.
Reject it: tool results must be appended to the conversation history so the model can reason over everything found so far.
questoes.explicacao: In the agentic loop, each tool result is appended to the conversation so the model can incorporate it into its next decision. Dropping earlier results leaves the model unable to compare sources, notice gaps, or avoid repeats. Trimming irrelevant fields from verbose results is fine; removing the results entirely is not.
feedbacks: Without earlier results the model cannot compare sources or avoid repeats; the saving costs the reasoning the loop exists for.
A list of queries prevents some repeats but hides what those searches returned, so the model cannot build on the findings.
Rerunning searches wastes calls and time and still leaves the model without the accumulated findings.
Correct. Tool results added to the context between iterations are what the model reasons over.

questoes.pergunta: Eastbrook University Library runs a multi-agent research system built with the Claude Agent SDK: a coordinator delegates to web search, document analysis, synthesis, and report-generation subagents to produce comprehensive, cited reports for faculty. For broad topics such as "climate migration policy in Southeast Asia", the coordinator spawns three web search subagents in parallel, each with the full question. About 60% of the sources they return overlap, so each report pays for the same searches several times. The team cannot add subagents or raise the per-report budget. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Have each search subagent check a shared list of URLs already read before each search, so it can skip sources another instance found.
Have the coordinator give each subagent a distinct slice of the scope, such as one source type each: government, academic, NGO.
Keep the identical prompts and have the synthesis subagent deduplicate the overlapping sources before it writes its synthesis.
Use a single search subagent with a longer time budget, so the research no longer produces any duplicated results to remove.
questoes.explicacao: When parallel subagents receive the same broad question, they search the same ground. Partitioning the research scope, by assigning distinct subtopics or source types to each subagent, minimizes duplication within the same number of subagents and the same budget.
feedbacks: Subagents do not share memory; a shared list adds coordination machinery and still starts every instance from the same broad question.
Correct. Assigning distinct subtopics or source types minimizes duplicated searching.
Deduplicating afterwards still pays for the redundant searches; the waste happens upstream.
Removing parallelism avoids duplicates but slows research and narrows coverage; partitioning keeps both.

questoes.pergunta: Eastbrook University Library runs a multi-agent research system built with the Claude Agent SDK: a coordinator delegates to web search, document analysis, synthesis, and report-generation subagents to produce comprehensive, cited reports for faculty. The document analysis subagent has three tools: search_catalog (the library's holdings), extract_citations, and summarize_document. Its system prompt says: "Whenever a request mentions a source or citation, search the catalog first." When asked to "extract all citations from the attached paper", it calls search_catalog in about 70% of runs. The tool descriptions were rewritten last week and clearly separate the three tools. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Add few-shot examples to the system prompt showing extract_citations being chosen for requests about citations inside an attached paper.
Rename extract_citations to pull_reference_list, so that its name no longer shares the word that triggers the catalog search.
Merge search_catalog and extract_citations into one citation tool that decides internally whether to search the catalog or to extract.
Rewrite the keyword-triggered instruction in the system prompt so it no longer overrides the tool descriptions for these requests.
questoes.explicacao: Keyword-sensitive instructions in a system prompt can create unintended tool associations that override well-written descriptions. The rule fires on the word 'citation' in the request, so the first step is to review and rewrite that instruction.
feedbacks: Examples would compete with the instruction rather than remove it; the instruction keeps pulling selection toward search_catalog.
The trigger is the word in the request, not in the tool's name; renaming the tool leaves the instruction firing on every mention of citations.
Consolidation hides the choice inside the tool and adds work; the descriptions are already clear, so overlap is not the problem.
Correct. Review system prompts for keyword-sensitive instructions that override good tool descriptions.

questoes.pergunta: Eastbrook University Library runs a multi-agent research system built with the Claude Agent SDK: a coordinator delegates to web search, document analysis, synthesis, and report-generation subagents to produce comprehensive, cited reports for faculty. A publisher's PDF server returns intermittent 503 errors on about 8% of downloads, and nearly all succeed on one retry. The team is choosing between two designs for the document analysis subagent. Design X: return every failure to the coordinator immediately. Design Y: retry transient failures locally and, if a document still fails, return a structured error with what was attempted and the analyses already completed. Which choice is best?
opcoes: Design Y: transient failures are fixed where they happen, and the coordinator gets only unresolved ones, with attempts and partial results.
Design X: the coordinator should make the retry decisions, because it is the only agent that can see the whole research plan.
Design Y, but without the partial analyses, since incomplete results could mislead the synthesis subagent about the coverage.
Design X, with the coordinator retrying each failed download three times before marking the document unavailable in the report.
questoes.explicacao: Subagents should recover locally from transient failures and propagate only the errors they cannot resolve. When they do propagate, including what was attempted and the partial results lets the coordinator decide whether to proceed, re-delegate, or note a gap.
feedbacks: Correct. Local recovery for transient failures, with structured escalation of what remains, keeps the coordinator informed without routine noise.
Routing routine 503s through the coordinator adds round trips and clutters its context; it needs only what the subagent could not fix.
Partial results are part of what lets the coordinator decide whether to proceed; dropping them forces wasteful re-work.
Retrying from the coordinator puts transient handling in the wrong layer and repeats a whole delegation for a network blip.

questoes.pergunta: Eastbrook University Library runs a multi-agent research system built with the Claude Agent SDK: a coordinator delegates to web search, document analysis, synthesis, and report-generation subagents to produce comprehensive, cited reports for faculty. Faculty find claims in recent reports, such as "remote instruction lowered course completion by 12%", with no citation. Tracing a run shows that the search subagent returned URLs and excerpts for every finding, but the coordinator condensed each subagent's output into a 200-word paragraph before passing it to the synthesis subagent. Which TWO statements best explain or fix this? Choose TWO.
opcoes: The coordinator's condensing step compresses findings into prose and drops the link between each claim and its source.
The synthesis subagent's prompt should require a citation for every claim, which on its own would restore the missing sources.
Citations are lost when the report-generation subagent formats the text, because that formatting step strips footnotes.
Upstream outputs should carry claim-source mappings (claim, URL or document, excerpt) that each later step preserves.
The coordinator should pass the full raw web pages to synthesis, so the synthesis subagent can work out the sources itself.
questoes.explicacao: Source attribution is lost when a summarization step compresses findings without preserving claim-source mappings. Structured mappings (claim, source URL or document, excerpt) that every downstream step must keep and merge prevent the loss.
feedbacks: Correct. Compressing findings into prose discards which source supports which claim.
Synthesis cannot cite what it no longer has; the mapping was destroyed before it arrived.
The trace shows the sources were already gone before synthesis; report formatting is not where they disappeared.
Correct. Structured claim-source mappings preserved through each step keep attribution intact.
Raw pages bloat context and force synthesis to redo attribution; structured mappings carry the same information compactly.

questoes.pergunta: Eastbrook University Library runs a multi-agent research system built with the Claude Agent SDK: a coordinator delegates to web search, document analysis, synthesis, and report-generation subagents to produce comprehensive, cited reports for faculty. In a report on open-access mandates, the web search subagent returned {"status": "failed"} for 3 of 9 queries, and the coordinator could not decide what to do next. The subagent's logs show that one query timed out after collecting 4 results, one was rejected by the search API as malformed, and one received a 403 from a subscription database. Which TWO statements are correct? Choose TWO.
opcoes: A generic status is preferable because it keeps the coordinator's context small; the details belong in the subagent's own logs.
With one generic status for all three, the coordinator cannot tell that one needs a retry, one a new query, and one another source.
The coordinator should treat a failed status as "no results" and move on, since most reports remain usable without those queries.
The subagent should retry the three with exponential backoff before replying, which makes reporting the failure details unnecessary.
The subagent should report each failure's type, the query attempted, partial results such as the 4 collected, and alternatives.
questoes.explicacao: Generic error statuses hide exactly the context the coordinator needs: a timeout, a malformed query, and a permission error call for different recoveries. Structured error context (failure type, attempted query, partial results, alternatives) enables those decisions.
feedbacks: The coordinator makes the recovery decisions; hiding the details in logs it cannot see defeats that.
Correct. A single generic status hides which recovery each failure needs.
Treating failures as empty results silently suppresses errors and leaves gaps the report will not disclose.
Backoff cannot fix a malformed query or a permission error, and the 4 partial results would still be lost.
Correct. Structured error context lets the coordinator retry, rephrase, or switch sources, and keep the partial results.

questoes.pergunta: Eastbrook University Library runs a multi-agent research system built with the Claude Agent SDK: a coordinator delegates to web search, document analysis, synthesis, and report-generation subagents to produce comprehensive, cited reports for faculty. The coordinator runs search, analysis, and synthesis once per request. When the synthesis output contains a "Gaps" section, the coordinator copies it into the report under "Limitations" and sends everything to the report-generation subagent. Faculty note that about 40% of reports list gaps such as "no data after 2021" that a single targeted search would have filled. What is the flaw?
opcoes: The coordinator accepts the gaps as final; it should re-delegate targeted queries for them and re-run synthesis until coverage suffices.
The synthesis subagent should run its own web searches when it finds a gap, so the coordinator does not have to be involved.
The coordinator should split the topic into more subtasks at the start, so that no gaps appear and a second round is never needed.
The pipeline should run the full search, analysis, and synthesis sequence twice for each request and merge the two outputs.
questoes.explicacao: The coordinator should evaluate synthesis output for gaps, re-delegate targeted queries to the search and analysis subagents, and re-invoke synthesis until coverage is sufficient. Copying the gaps into the report skips that iterative refinement loop.
feedbacks: Correct. An iterative refinement loop closes the gaps that a single pass leaves.
Giving synthesis search tools invites cross-specialization misuse and bypasses the coordinator's control of the research.
Broader upfront decomposition helps, but some gaps only show up after synthesis; a refinement loop is what catches them.
Repeating the same untargeted pipeline doubles the cost without aiming at the gaps it found.

questoes.pergunta: Eastbrook University Library runs a multi-agent research system built with the Claude Agent SDK: a coordinator delegates to web search, document analysis, synthesis, and report-generation subagents to produce comprehensive, cited reports for faculty. The system handles two request types: citation audits of theses (check each chapter's references for format, retractions, and broken links) and exploratory literature questions. After the team switched both types from a fixed pipeline to dynamic decomposition, exploratory reports improved, but citation audits became erratic: 15% skipped a check, and run times now vary threefold. Which statement about this outcome is correct?
opcoes: Citation audits are predictable checks that suit a fixed pipeline, while open questions suit dynamic decomposition; use each where it fits.
Both types should keep dynamic decomposition, adding a coordinator prompt that lists each audit check the plan has to include.
Both types should go back to the fixed pipeline, because the improvement in exploratory reports is most likely run-to-run noise.
The erratic audits come from the coordinator's model; a larger model would make dynamic plans as consistent as a fixed pipeline.
questoes.explicacao: Fixed sequential pipelines (prompt chaining) suit predictable, multi-step work like citation audits; dynamic adaptive decomposition suits open-ended investigation. The outcome shows each pattern helping where it fits and hurting where it does not, so the system should route each request type to its own pattern.
feedbacks: Correct. Match the decomposition pattern to the workflow: chaining for predictable checks, adaptive decomposition for open questions.
Listing the checks makes a fixed procedure depend on probabilistic planning; a fixed pipeline runs every check by construction.
Reverting discards a real improvement for exploratory work, which benefits from subtasks generated by intermediate findings.
A larger model still plans afresh on every run; predictable checks do not need planning at all.

questoes.pergunta: Eastbrook University Library runs a multi-agent research system built with the Claude Agent SDK: a coordinator delegates to web search, document analysis, synthesis, and report-generation subagents to produce comprehensive, cited reports for faculty. The document analysis subagent uses the MCP tools load_document and extract_tables. Today their errors distinguish a timeout, a malformed page range, a document outside the library's license, and a corrupt file. To simplify the server, an engineer proposes that every failure return {"isError": true, "content": "Operation failed"}, arguing that the agent "only needs to know the call failed." How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Reject it: a uniform message hides whether a timeout, a bad page range, or a license limit occurred, so the agent cannot pick a recovery.
Accept it: the agent's recovery is the same for each failure (retry once, then report), so detailed error categories would only add tokens.
Accept it, provided the server logs each full exception, so engineers can still diagnose failures when they review the logs later.
Reject it, and return the raw exception text from the PDF library instead, since that text already holds everything the agent would ever need.
questoes.explicacao: Uniform error responses prevent the agent from making appropriate recovery decisions. A timeout may succeed on retry, a malformed page range needs corrected input, and a license restriction will never succeed; the agent can act correctly only if the error says which one occurred.
feedbacks: Correct. Each error category implies a different action, which a generic message erases.
Retrying a license restriction or a malformed range can never succeed; one recovery path for every failure wastes calls and time.
Logs help engineers later but give the agent nothing to decide with at runtime.
Raw library text is unstructured and inconsistent; the agent needs a category and a retryable signal it can act on.

questoes.pergunta: Eastbrook University Library runs a multi-agent research system built with the Claude Agent SDK: a coordinator delegates to web search, document analysis, synthesis, and report-generation subagents to produce comprehensive, cited reports for faculty. The coordinator invokes the synthesis subagent through the Task tool with the prompt: "Synthesize the findings from the search and document analysis steps on rural broadband adoption into a report draft." The draft is a generic overview that cites none of the 23 documents analyzed earlier in the run. The team cannot add shared storage or new tools. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Give the synthesis subagent the web search tools, so that it can collect again whatever material it needs to write a well-cited report draft.
Add to the synthesis subagent's system prompt: "Use the earlier findings carefully and cite every document that was analyzed."
Have the coordinator put the complete search results and document analyses, with their sources, directly in the synthesis Task prompt.
Run synthesis by resuming the document analysis subagent's session, so the synthesis step inherits the context that already holds the analyses.
questoes.explicacao: Subagents do not inherit the coordinator's context or share memory; whatever they need must be passed explicitly in their prompt. Including the complete findings from prior agents, with their sources, in the synthesis subagent's Task prompt gives it the material to synthesize and cite.
feedbacks: Re-collecting duplicates work and gives synthesis tools outside its role; the findings already exist in the coordinator.
Telling the subagent to use findings it never received cannot work; it has no implicit access to them.
Correct. Pass prior agents' complete findings directly in the subagent's prompt.
Reusing another subagent's session mixes roles and still omits the search results; explicit context passing is the intended mechanism.

questoes.pergunta: Eastbrook University Library runs a multi-agent research system built with the Claude Agent SDK: a coordinator delegates to web search, document analysis, synthesis, and report-generation subagents to produce comprehensive, cited reports for faculty. For a report that needs six independent PDFs analyzed, the coordinator's logs show one Task call to the document analysis subagent per response: it waits for each result before issuing the next call. Analysis accounts for 18 of the 24 minutes a report takes. What is the most effective first step to cut this time?
opcoes: Send the six PDFs to the document analysis subagent in one Task call, so a single instance analyzes them back to back in one shared context.
Have the coordinator emit the six Task calls in a single response, so the analyses run in parallel and their results return together.
Set the coordinator's tool_choice to "any", so it calls a tool on every turn instead of pausing to write text between delegations.
Move the six analyses to the Message Batches API, which processes many requests at once and costs about half as much per document.
questoes.explicacao: Subagents are spawned in parallel when the coordinator emits multiple Task tool calls in a single response, rather than one per turn. The six independent analyses then run concurrently, removing most of the sequential wait.
feedbacks: One instance processing six PDFs is still sequential and packs every document into one context.
Correct. Multiple Task calls in one coordinator response run the subagents in parallel.
tool_choice controls whether a tool is called, not whether calls are issued together; the coordinator would still delegate one per turn.
Batches cut cost but offer no latency guarantee (up to 24 hours), which would make a 24-minute report far slower.

questoes.pergunta: Eastbrook University Library runs a multi-agent research system built with the Claude Agent SDK: a coordinator delegates to web search, document analysis, synthesis, and report-generation subagents to produce comprehensive, cited reports for faculty. Each handoff through the coordinator adds about 10 seconds. To cut latency, an engineer proposes letting the web search subagent send its results straight to the synthesis subagent, and synthesis send its draft straight to report generation, with the coordinator receiving only the final report. Which design should the team choose?
opcoes: The direct handoffs: removing the coordinator from the data path cuts latency, and it can still check quality on the final report.
Keep routing through the coordinator: handoffs stay observable, errors are handled consistently, and it controls what each gets.
The direct handoffs, with each subagent writing a log entry for each message it sends, which gives the same visibility as the hub.
A hybrid: keep the coordinator only for error handling and let subagents exchange results directly, balancing latency and control.
questoes.explicacao: Routing all subagent communication through the coordinator provides observability, consistent error handling, and controlled information flow. Direct handoffs save seconds but remove the point where gaps, errors, and missing sources can be caught and where the coordinator decides what each subagent receives.
feedbacks: Checking only the final report loses the chance to catch gaps, errors, and missing sources at each step, when they are cheap to fix.
Correct. Hub-and-spoke routing keeps every handoff visible and under the coordinator's control.
Logs give after-the-fact visibility but no control: nobody decides what flows between subagents or how failures are handled.
Splitting responsibilities leaves the coordinator handling errors for data it never saw and unable to control what each subagent receives.

questoes.pergunta: Eastbrook University Library runs a multi-agent research system built with the Claude Agent SDK: a coordinator delegates to web search, document analysis, synthesis, and report-generation subagents to produce comprehensive, cited reports for faculty. The provost's office requires reports to show readers where credible sources disagree. For the 2023 graduating cohort, a government survey reports that 34% of graduates carry more than $30,000 in student debt, while a national university study reports 41%. The synthesis subagent currently keeps the figure from the more recent publication and cites only that source. What should change to meet the requirement?
opcoes: Have the synthesis subagent average the two conflicting values and cite both sources for the averaged figure in the report.
Have the synthesis subagent report both values with their sources and methods, marking the claim as contested.
Have the synthesis subagent keep the source with the larger sample size and move the other value into a footnote.
Have the coordinator search until a third source breaks the tie, then report the value supported by most of the sources.
questoes.explicacao: When credible sources report conflicting statistics, the synthesis should annotate the conflict with source attribution instead of selecting one value. Reporting both figures with their sources and methodology, and marking the claim as contested, is what lets readers see the disagreement.
feedbacks: An average is a number neither source reported, and it hides the disagreement the requirement asks to show.
Correct. Annotate conflicting values with their sources rather than choosing one.
Sample size is one quality signal, but selecting by it still hides a credible disagreement from readers.
Majority voting across sources is still arbitrary selection, and it spends extra searches to hide the conflict.

questoes.pergunta: Eastbrook University Library runs a multi-agent research system built with the Claude Agent SDK: a coordinator delegates to web search, document analysis, synthesis, and report-generation subagents to produce comprehensive, cited reports for faculty. The library's license with one publisher allows at most 50 full-text downloads per day through its API. The limit is stated in the system prompts of the web search and document analysis subagents and in the description of their load_document tool. Last month the publisher flagged four days with 63 to 90 downloads; on ordinary days the system stays under the limit. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: The limit exists only as prompt text, which is followed probabilistically; nothing intercepts load_document calls and blocks those over the cap.
The load_document description is too long, so the limit is lost among other details; moving it into the first sentence would fix it.
The subagents cannot see the running count; injecting the day's download total into each prompt would let them stop at 50.
The coordinator runs too many subagents in parallel on busy days; limiting it to one at a time would keep downloads under the cap.
questoes.explicacao: A compliance rule that must always hold cannot rely on prompt instructions, which models follow probabilistically. A hook that intercepts outgoing load_document calls, counts downloads, and blocks calls above the daily limit enforces the license deterministically, however many subagents run.
feedbacks: Correct. Hooks that intercept outgoing tool calls turn a compliance rule into a guarantee; prompt text cannot.
Placement may improve salience but leaves compliance probabilistic; the busy-day overruns show instructions alone fail.
Giving the model the count still relies on it choosing to stop, and parallel subagents can exceed the cap between updates.
Less parallelism slows research for everyone and still does not enforce the limit; a sequential run can exceed 50 too.

questoes.pergunta: Eastbrook University Library runs a multi-agent research system built with the Claude Agent SDK: a coordinator delegates to web search, document analysis, synthesis, and report-generation subagents to produce comprehensive, cited reports for faculty. The document analysis subagent was given a generic fetch_url(url) tool so it could open articles from the catalog. Logs show it also fetching news homepages, search-engine result pages, and a 300 MB dataset file, which fill its context and slow runs by several minutes. What is the flaw in this design?
opcoes: The subagent's system prompt does not restrict what it fetches; adding "fetch only scholarly documents" would stop the stray requests.
The subagent should not fetch anything; the search subagent should download each document and pass its full text in the Task prompt.
It has a generic fetch tool where it needs a constrained one, such as a load_document tool that accepts only validated document URLs.
fetch_url has no size limit; capping downloads at 20 MB would stop the large files from filling the analysis subagent's context.
questoes.explicacao: A generic tool gives a subagent capabilities beyond its role, and it will use them. Replacing fetch_url with a constrained load_document tool that validates document URLs keeps the subagent on scholarly documents by design rather than by instruction.
feedbacks: A prompt restriction is probabilistic and leaves the generic capability in place; the tool itself should constrain what can be fetched.
Moving all downloading to search makes Task prompts enormous and shifts the problem; the analysis role does need to load documents.
Correct. Replace generic tools with constrained alternatives that validate their inputs.
A size cap stops the dataset file but not the news and search pages; the tool still accepts any URL.

questoes.pergunta: Eastbrook University Library runs a multi-agent research system built with the Claude Agent SDK: a coordinator delegates to web search, document analysis, synthesis, and report-generation subagents to produce comprehensive, cited reports for faculty. The report-generation subagent often needs to confirm that a citation's DOI resolves and that its authors and year match before it formats the bibliography. Each time, it hands control back to the coordinator, which calls the web search subagent and then re-invokes report generation, adding about three round trips per report. Most checks are simple metadata lookups; a few involve disputed authorship or retracted papers. Which TWO changes best reduce the overhead while keeping the system reliable? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Give the report-generation subagent a scoped verify_citation tool that resolves a DOI and returns its title, authors, and year.
Give the report-generation subagent the full web search toolset, so it can settle citation questions itself without the coordinator.
Have the report-generation subagent skip verification and mark unchecked citations, so faculty can confirm them while reading.
Have the search subagent pre-verify each source's DOI during the initial research, anticipating what report generation will check.
Keep sending disputed-authorship and retraction cases back through the coordinator to the search and analysis subagents.
questoes.explicacao: A scoped cross-role tool covers the high-frequency simple case (resolving a DOI and its metadata) without round trips. Complex cases such as disputed authorship or retractions still go through the coordinator, preserving the specialization and control of the hub-and-spoke design.
feedbacks: Correct. A scoped verify tool handles the frequent simple lookups directly.
Full search access over-provisions the subagent, invites cross-specialization misuse, and bypasses coordinator control for complex cases.
Pushing verification to readers lowers report quality and shifts the work onto faculty.
Speculative pre-verification spends work on sources that may never be cited and cannot anticipate every check.
Correct. Complex cases keep routing through the coordinator, which the scoped tool does not replace.

questoes.pergunta: Eastbrook University Library runs a multi-agent research system built with the Claude Agent SDK: a coordinator delegates to web search, document analysis, synthesis, and report-generation subagents to produce comprehensive, cited reports for faculty. For a report on campus housing affordability, the coordinator spent about 40 minutes building a shared analysis of 60 sources. Faculty now want two versions built on that baseline: one framed as recommendations for policy-makers and one as a methodological review. An engineer proposes running the whole pipeline twice from scratch with different instructions. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Adopt it: running from scratch guarantees that each version is fully independent and not biased by the other version's reasoning.
